title: Time & aspect edge cases
note: future perfect vs future perfect continuous from a named future point · be to / be due to for official arrangement, including the passive · future in the past: was to, was to have + PP, was about to, was on the point of · aspect that is not about time: always/forever/constantly + continuous, keep + -ing, state verbs in the continuous · 4 strands x 12 · 48 items · built to live 2026-08-07 (cloud run 11)

items.en: By June I will have been teaching here for twenty years.
items.cz: V červnu tu budu učit už dvacet let.
items.gap: By June I ____ here for twenty years.
accepts: By June I will have been teaching here for twenty years.
By June I'll have been teaching here for twenty years.
items.explanation: From a point in the future both forms look back. The continuous says how long the activity will have been running; the simple reports the finished result, or how much will be done. State verbs have no continuous.

cards.title: The edges of future and aspect
cards.body: You already have will, going to and the present forms for the future. This unit takes the four places where English needs something else: a vantage point inside the future, a formal arrangement, a plan that never happened, and a continuous form that is not about time at all.
cards.body_cz: will, going to i přítomné tvary pro budoucnost už umíte. Tato lekce bere čtyři místa, kde angličtina potřebuje něco jiného: pohled z bodu uvnitř budoucnosti, formální plán, plán, který se neuskutečnil, a průběhový tvar, který o čase nevypovídá vůbec nic.

table.caption: the four edges
rows: looking back from the future
will have (been) + …
By June I will have been teaching here for twenty years.
official arrangement
be to · be due to
The president is to visit Prague in October.
the plan that failed
was to have + past participle
He was to have spoken, but he was ill.
not about time
always / keep + -ing
He keeps interrupting me.

points: Each one is a choice of meaning, not a new tense to memorise.

cards.title: How long, or how much — seen from the future
cards.title_cz: Jak dlouho, nebo kolik — pohledem z budoucnosti
cards.body: Stand at a point in the future and look back. The continuous measures the run of the activity; the simple reports the result.
cards.body_cz: Postavte se do bodu v budoucnosti a ohlédněte se. Průběhový tvar měří průběh činnosti; prostý oznamuje výsledek.

table.caption: the pair
rows: When you arrive, we will have been driving for six hours.
By tonight they will have driven from Prague to Vienna.
This time next month I will have been studying Spanish for a year.
By the end of the week she will have written four reports.

points: The point in the future must be named: by June, when you arrive, this time next month.
State verbs stay simple: By Friday he will have known her for exactly a year, never `will have been knowing`.

cards.title: be to and be due to
cards.title_cz: be to a be due to
cards.body: be to + base verb is the formal future of arrangement, instruction and news reporting. be due to names the scheduled moment. Both sound official — in speech you would use will or going to instead.
cards.body_cz: be to + základní tvar je formální budoucnost plánu, pokynu a zpráv. be due to udává plánovaný okamžik. Obojí zní úředně — v běžné řeči byste použili will nebo going to.
points: News: The president is to visit Prague in October.
Instruction: You are to report to the manager at nine.
Timetable: The train is due to arrive at half past six.
Passive is very common: The results are to be published next week.
Condition of purpose: If you are to pass the exam, you must start now.

cards.title: The plan that never happened
cards.body: Move be to into the past and it reports what was arranged — or what fate had in store. Add have + past participle and it says the arrangement was never carried out.
cards.body_cz: Přesuňte be to do minulosti a hlásí, co bylo domluveno — nebo co chystal osud. Přidejte have + příčestí minulé a věta říká, že se plán nikdy neuskutečnil.

table.caption: arranged, and unfulfilled
rows: We were to meet at twelve.
He was to have spoken, but he was ill.
He was to become a famous writer.
The money was to have been paid last month.

points: was about to / was on the point of + -ing = the moment just before it.
was never to see = fate, not arrangement — a literary use.

cards.title: When the continuous is not about time
cards.title_cz: Když průběhový tvar není o čase
cards.body: With always, forever or constantly, the continuous stops reporting time and starts carrying irritation. keep + -ing does the same for repetition. And a state verb in the continuous changes meaning.
cards.body_cz: S always, forever nebo constantly přestává průběhový tvar sdělovat čas a začíná nést podráždění. keep + -ing dělá totéž u opakování. A stavové sloveso v průběhovém tvaru mění význam.

table.caption: state verb, two meanings
rows: He is difficult.
He is being difficult today.
They have a garden.
They are having lunch in the garden.
I see the problem.
She is seeing someone new.

points: She always drinks coffee = a habit. She is always complaining = a complaint about her.
keep + -ing, never keep + to: He keeps interrupting me.

cards.title: Common mistakes

table.caption: check
rows: By Friday he will have been knowing her for a year.
By Friday he will have known her for exactly a year.
The train is due arrive at half past six.
The train is due to arrive at half past six.
He was to speak, but he was ill.
He was to have spoken, but he was ill.
He keeps to interrupt me.
He keeps interrupting me.
My colleagues keeps changing the plan.
My colleagues keep changing the plan.
She is always complain about the traffic.
She is always complaining about the traffic.

points: Czech has one future and no continuous, so every one of these is a meaning choice, not a translation.
be to is formal. Do not use it for your own plans — that is going to.
